title: The Anion Gap Detective: Gap, Albumin, Delta and Osmoles
summary: Calculate and interpret the anion gap with method-specific ranges and albumin correction, check respiratory compensation with Winter’s formula, use the delta ratio to find a second disorder, and use the osmolal gap to suspect toxic alcohols.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 15 Hit 3 (anion gap), Hit 4 (albumin correction), Hit 5 (delta gap/ratio), Hit 6 (Winter’s formula), Hit 7 (high-gap causes; the MUDPILES list itself is not reproduced), Hit 9 (osmolality and osmolal gap) and Trap 1. Checked against Lee 2006, Korus 2025, Eraky 2026, Azzam 2026, Messersmith 2024, Paliwal 2022, Ahmed 2020 and Nogueira 2026. The reviewer’s “normal ≈ 12 (8–16)” is method-dependent (register flag rv-ag-normal). The reviewer’s delta-ratio bands (< 0.4, 0.4–0.8, 0.8–2.0, > 2.0) were not found in the sources read; sources used < 1 for an added normal-gap acidosis and > 1.2 for an added metabolic alkalosis, so the lesson teaches “< 1” and “well above 1”.

objectives: Calculate the anion gap and interpret it against a method-specific reference range.
Correct the anion gap for hypoalbuminemia.
Check respiratory compensation with Winter’s formula and use the delta ratio to detect a second metabolic disorder.
Calculate the osmolal gap and explain why it can be normal late after toxic alcohol ingestion.

scenes.title: One acidosis — or three?
scenes.altText: A patient card: found confused, slurred speech, smells of nothing. A blood-gas card: pH 7.18, HCO₃⁻ 8 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 22 mmHg. A chemistry card: Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 104, glucose 90 mg/dL, BUN 28 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL; measured osmolality 320 mOsm/kg. Question tokens: “Which kind of acidosis?”, “Is the lungs’ response right?”, “Anything hidden?”.

cues.text: A confused patient arrives. The blood gas shows a pH of 7.18 and a bicarbonate of only 8.
The chemistry panel and a measured osmolality come back too. Four simple calculations will turn these numbers into a diagnosis.
Which kind of acidosis is it? Are the lungs compensating properly? And is a second disorder hiding underneath?

scenes.title: The anion gap — and why its “normal” moves
scenes.altText: Two bars: a sodium bar (140) next to a stacked bar of chloride (104) plus bicarbonate (24). The space left over is the anion gap — unmeasured anions, mostly albumin. Formula token: AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). A reference card: older flame/colorimetric methods 12 ± 4; ion-selective electrodes 6 ± 3 mmol/L; use your laboratory’s range. An albumin card: low albumin lowers the gap — add about 2.5 for every 1 g/dL below normal (4.0; some use 4.5).

cues.text: Blood is electrically neutral. Sodium, the main cation, is balanced by chloride, bicarbonate and anions we do not measure.
The anion gap is sodium minus chloride plus bicarbonate. The gap is mostly albumin and other unmeasured anions.
Its normal range depends on the method. With older methods it was about 12, plus or minus 4; with ion-selective electrodes it fell to about 6, plus or minus 3. Use your lab’s range.
Albumin is the biggest unmeasured anion. When albumin is low, the gap shrinks, and a real acidosis can hide.
So correct it: add about 2.5 to the gap for every gram per deciliter that albumin is below normal, usually 4.0, though some use 4.5.

scenes.title: A high gap has many causes — and some leave osmoles
scenes.altText: A high-gap card lists causes: kidney failure, lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, methanol, glycols, aspirin (salicylate), 5-oxoproline, D-lactate. A “not just lactate” highlight. Then the osmolality formula: calculated = 2 × Na⁺ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (+ ethanol/3.7). Osmolal gap = measured − calculated; > 10 mOsm/kg suggests an unmeasured osmole such as methanol or ethylene glycol. A timeline token: as the alcohol is metabolized to acids, the osmolal gap falls while the anion gap rises.

cues.text: A high anion gap means extra unmeasured acid anions. The common causes are kidney failure, lactic acidosis and ketoacidosis.
But toxic alcohols, glycols, aspirin, 5-oxoproline and D-lactate also raise the gap. A high gap is not automatically lactate.
The osmolal gap helps with toxic alcohols. Calculated osmolality is two times sodium, plus glucose over 18, plus BUN over 2.8.
Measured minus calculated is the osmolal gap. More than about 10 suggests an unmeasured osmole, such as methanol or ethylene glycol. Ethanol raises it too.
Timing matters. As the alcohol is metabolized into acids, the osmolal gap falls while the anion gap rises, so a late sample can show a near-normal osmolal gap.

scenes.title: Solving the patient: gap, Winter’s, delta, osmoles
scenes.altText: Step cards fill in for the patient. Gap: 140 − (104 + 8) = 28 (albumin normal, so no correction). Winter’s formula: expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × 8 + 8 = 20 ± 2 → 18–22; measured 22 → appropriate compensation (higher would mean an added respiratory acidosis). Delta ratio (using 12 and 24 as the normal midpoints): ΔAG 16 ÷ ΔHCO₃⁻ 16 = 1.0 → a pure high-gap acidosis; < 1 would mean an added normal-gap acidosis, well above 1 (one source: > 1.2) an added metabolic alkalosis. Osmoles: calculated 2 × 140 + 90/18 + 28/2.8 = 295; measured 320; gap 25 → suspect a toxic alcohol (e.g., methanol). Confirm with a specific level.

cues.text: Step one, the gap: 140 minus 104 plus 8 is 28. Albumin is normal, so no correction is needed. It is a high-gap acidosis.
Step two, Winter’s formula: expected PaCO₂ is 1.5 times bicarbonate plus 8, plus or minus 2. Here 18 to 22. The measured 22 fits: compensation is appropriate.
Step three, the delta ratio: how much the gap rose, divided by how much bicarbonate fell. 16 over 16 is 1, so no hidden second metabolic disorder.
If the ratio were below 1, bicarbonate fell more than the gap rose: an added normal-gap acidosis. Well above 1 suggests an added metabolic alkalosis.
Step four, the osmoles: calculated 295, measured 320, a gap of 25. Suspect a toxic alcohol, and confirm with a specific level.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards appear in turn: “A high anion gap means lactic acidosis” (✓ also kidney failure, ketoacidosis, toxic alcohols, aspirin, 5-oxoproline, D-lactate); “A normal anion gap is 12 everywhere” (✓ method-dependent — ion-selective electrodes ~6 ± 3; use the lab’s range); “A normal osmolal gap rules out a toxic alcohol” (✓ the gap falls as the alcohol is metabolized).

cues.text: Trap one: a high anion gap means lactic acidosis. Not necessarily. Kidney failure, ketoacids, toxic alcohols, aspirin and others raise it too.
Trap two: the normal anion gap is 12 everywhere. No. It depends on the method; with ion-selective electrodes it is about 6, plus or minus 3.
Trap three: a normal osmolal gap rules out a toxic alcohol. No. As the alcohol is metabolized, the osmolal gap falls and the anion gap rises.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) · use the lab’s range · +2.5 per g/dL albumin deficit”, “Winter’s 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 · delta ratio < 1 = added normal-gap acidosis · osmolal gap > 10 = look for toxic alcohol”.

cues.text: Calculate the anion gap against your lab’s range and correct it for albumin, then use Winter’s formula, the delta ratio and the osmolal gap to uncover what else is going on.

props.label: AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) · lab’s own range · +2.5 per g/dL albumin deficit
Winter’s 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 · Δ ratio < 1 → + normal-gap acidosis · osm gap > 10 → toxic alcohol?

explanation.what: Plain language: the anion gap is the electrical space left over when you subtract the measured anions from sodium; when it grows, an extra acid is present. Scientific terms: AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA); albumin-corrected AG; Winter’s formula; delta ratio = ΔAG/ΔHCO₃⁻; calculated osmolality and osmolal gap.
explanation.why: Unmeasured acid anions (lactate, ketoacids, toxic alcohol metabolites, uremic anions) replace bicarbonate and widen the gap. Albumin is the main normal unmeasured anion, so low albumin narrows the gap and can mask HAGMA. Toxic alcohols are osmotically active before they are metabolized to acids.
explanation.measure: Normal AG: method-dependent (flame/colorimetric 12 ± 4; ion-selective electrodes 6 ± 3 mmol/L; one 2025 review 4–12). Corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL). Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2. Delta ratio = (AG − 12)/(24 − HCO₃⁻). Calculated osmolality = 2 × Na⁺ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (+ ethanol/3.7); osmolal gap > 10 mOsm/kg elevated.
explanation.differs: High-gap vs normal-gap acidosis; appropriate compensation vs added respiratory acidosis (PaCO₂ higher than expected); delta ratio < 1 (added normal-gap acidosis) vs well above 1 (added metabolic alkalosis); early (high osmolal gap) vs late (high anion gap) toxic alcohol.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate AG and corrected AG, apply Winter’s formula, interpret a delta ratio, calculate an osmolal gap, and avoid equating every high gap with lactate.

questions.stem: Na⁺ 135, Cl⁻ 100, HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L; albumin 2.0 g/dL. What is the albumin-corrected anion gap (normal albumin 4.0 g/dL)?

options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the uncorrected gap; low albumin hides part of it.
Incorrect. The correction is added, not subtracted.
Incorrect. The correction is about 2.5 per g/dL, so 5, not 10.

questions.stem: Metabolic acidosis: HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L, PaCO₂ 32 mmHg. What does Winter’s formula indicate?

options.rationale: Correct. Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × 12 + 8 = 26 ± 2 (24–28); 32 is higher, so ventilation is inadequate.
Incorrect. 32 is outside the expected 24–28 mmHg.
Incorrect. The PaCO₂ is above, not below, the expected range; the lungs are under-ventilating.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate is low, not high.

questions.stem: AG 24 mmol/L and HCO₃⁻ 8 mmol/L (normal midpoints 12 and 24). What does the delta ratio suggest?

options.text: High-gap acidosis plus a normal-gap acidosis
options.rationale: Correct. ΔAG 12 ÷ ΔHCO₃⁻ 16 = 0.75 (< 1): bicarbonate fell more than the gap rose.
Incorrect. A pure high-gap acidosis gives a ratio near 1 or a little above.
Incorrect. That gives a ratio well above 1.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate is markedly low and the gap is high.

references.citation: Almoradie A. MEMORY LAB: The Memory-First Medical Laboratory Science Reviewer. 1st ed., v2.0. 2026. Chapter 15, Kidney Function, Electrolytes and Acid–Base (EPUB; no fixed page numbers).
references.usedFor: Curriculum source: scope and exam framing. Not used as verification.

references.citation: Lee S, Kang KP, Kang SK. Clinical usefulness of the serum anion gap. Electrolyte Blood Press. 2006;4(1):44-46.
references.usedFor: Normal anion gap 12 ± 4 mEq/L with flame photometry/colorimetric chloride; ion-selective electrodes shifted it to 6 ± 3 mEq/L; clinicians should know their laboratory’s range and methods; a high gap is almost always retained unmeasured anions.

references.citation: Korus J, Szymczak M, Gołębiowski M, et al. Metabolic acidosis in patients with chronic kidney disease: diagnosis, pathogenesis, and treatment — a narrative review. Diagnostics (Basel). 2025;15(16):2052.
references.usedFor: AG reference 4–12 mmol/L in its table; corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (4.0 − albumin g/dL); hypoalbuminemia masks a high gap; Winter’s formula PaCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8) ± 2, higher PaCO₂ = impaired respiratory response; HAGMA causes: kidney failure, lactic acidosis, DKA, glycols, 5-oxoproline, L- and D-lactate, methanol, aspirin.

references.citation: Eraky AM, Mokhtar Y, Grabau G, et al. Hypovolemic shock in the setting of third spacing with concentric left ventricular hypertrophy: a physiology-guided case. Pathophysiology. 2026;33(2):27.
references.usedFor: Add 2.5 to the AG per g of albumin below 4.5 g/dL (alternative reference); delta ratio = ΔAG/ΔHCO₃⁻; < 1 indicates coexisting normal-gap and high-gap acidosis.

references.citation: Azzam SKA, Barhoum LB, AbuRajab S, et al. Severe euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis with mixed acid-base disorder following acetazolamide initiation. Oxf Med Case Reports. 2026;2026(5):omag058.
references.usedFor: Delta ratio calculated as (AG − 12)/(24 − HCO₃⁻); 0.64 indicated mixed high-gap and normal-gap metabolic acidosis.

references.citation: Messersmith, Bayrakdar, Killeen. A case of diabetic ketoacidosis obscured by metabolic alkalosis in an individual with end-stage renal disease [abstract 9326]. J Endocr Soc. 2024;8(Suppl 1):bvae163.637.
references.usedFor: Delta ratio (increase in anion gap ÷ decrease in bicarbonate) greater than 1.2 in diabetic ketoacidosis with metabolic alkalosis.

references.citation: Paliwal R, Pakavakis A, Divatia JV, Kulkarni AP. Utility of Stewart’s approach to diagnose missed complex acid-base disorders as compared to bicarbonate-anion gap-based methodology in critically ill patients. Indian J Crit Care Med. 2022;26(1):23-32.
references.usedFor: Delta gap and delta ratio used to identify mixed disturbances; albumin-corrected AG; Stewart approach as an alternative method.

references.citation: Ahmed M, Janikowski C, Huda S, Ahmad A, Morrow L. Ethylene glycol poisoning with a near-normal osmolal gap: a diagnostic challenge. Cureus. 2020;12(12):e11937.
references.usedFor: Calculated serum osmolality = 2 × Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (+ ethanol/3.7); osmolal gap > 10 mOsm/kg elevated; metabolism of methanol or ethylene glycol causes a progressive decline in the osmolal gap; a near-normal osmolal gap can delay diagnosis.

references.citation: Nogueira GN, Teles CBM, Varão MVS, et al. Methanol intoxication and acute kidney injury: pathophysiological mechanisms and therapeutic approaches. J Bras Nefrol. 2026;48(3):e20250344.
references.usedFor: Methanol produces a marked osmolal gap (50 mg/dL ≈ +17 mOsm/kg); ethanol raises serum osmolality; ADH-blockade criteria include an osmolal gap > 10 mOsm/L with a documented ingestion.

claims.text: AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal range method-dependent (12 ± 4 older methods; 6 ± 3 ion-selective electrodes); use the lab’s range.
Low albumin lowers the AG and can mask HAGMA; add ~2.5 per g/dL below 4.0 (some use 4.5).
High-gap causes include kidney failure, lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, methanol, glycols, aspirin, 5-oxoproline and D-lactate.
Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2; higher = added respiratory acidosis.
Delta ratio = (AG − 12)/(24 − HCO₃⁻); < 1 indicates an added normal-gap acidosis; well above 1 (> 1.2 in one source) an added metabolic alkalosis.
Calculated osmolality = 2 × Na⁺ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 (+ ethanol/3.7); osmolal gap > 10 elevated; falls as toxic alcohol is metabolized; methanol raises it.
PaCO₂ lower than Winter’s expected value indicates an added respiratory alkalosis; reviewer’s delta-ratio bands < 0.4 / 0.4–0.8 / 0.8–2.0 / > 2.0.
